summary.text:
The most interesting single number in the batch. Cherwell was paid £14.6m to leave a 50-year PWLB loan, and is amortising it over ten years at £1.459m a year into an Interest Rate Equalisation reserve. That is the exact opposite of what nearly every other annual report this year says — that premiums make rescheduling unattractive — and the reason is visible in the loan book: fourteen PWLB loans priced between 1.29% and 2.99%.

We hold all fourteen and they tie to their Table 4 on every principal, rate and maturity date. £114m at a weighted 2.40%. On the DMO's curve this afternoon every one of them prices below par, about £9.56m in total. No CFR is published — the accounts are not finalised — so nothing about internal borrowing can be said.

The other thing worth noticing is that a quarter of the book, £36m, is short-dated local authority money at 4.15%–4.35%, while they are lending £4m to Bedford at 6.42% and £5m to Surrey Heath at 5.50% against money market funds paying 3.71%–3.84%. They are on both sides of the inter-authority market at a spread of more than two points.

officer.body:
Hi Janet,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the outturn report that went to Council on 20 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, because it came out unusually clean. We hold all fourteen of your PWLB loans and every one of them matches Table 4 on principal, rate and maturity date — the 6 at 1.29% to September 2026, the 16 at 2.90% to July 2031, the £5m at 2.50% running to 31 May 2048 that paragraph 3.5.4 calls the last one out. £114m at a weighted 2.40%. We also rebuilt all five buckets of Table 5 from Table 4 and they tie: £36m, £10m, £47m, £46m and £5m, summing to £144m against your 25/7/33/32/3.

One thing on our side to flag rather than yours: our file carries a fifteenth row, £5m at 5.13% maturing 10 June 2026, that isn't in Table 4. That is ours to check, not something for you to explain.

Now the part we wrote about. Paragraph 3.3 records a £14.6m discount from the PWLB on the early repayment of a 50-year loan, amortised over ten years at £1.459m a year. Almost every annual report we read this year says the opposite — that premiums on early repayment make rescheduling unattractive — and the reason yours went the other way is sitting in Table 4. A coupon below the premature repayment rate produces a discount rather than a premium, and fourteen of your loans are priced between 1.29% and 2.99%.

Which means it isn't a one-off. On the DMO's premature repayment curve this afternoon, notice 314/26, every one of the fourteen prices below par. About £9.56m across the book, on our numbers: roughly £1.89m of it on the 2.50% loan to 2048, another £1.15m on the £15m at 2.99% to 2032, and it thins out as you come down the curve. We're not suggesting you do anything with that — we don't sell treasury products and we've no view on whether any of it is worth acting on, which depends entirely on replacement cost and on the accounting, neither of which we model. What we'd say is only that the position is now a page you look at rather than a piece of work you commission. We price every council's book daily on the DMO's own formula — 182.5-day denominator, D+1 count, banker's rounding, the lot — and yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Ours is indicative; the DMO's is the only quote that binds.

The other thing that caught our eye is Table 8 next to Table 4. A quarter of your book, £36m, is short-dated local authority money at 4.15% to 4.35% — Middlesbrough, Lincolnshire twice, West Yorkshire Combined Authority, South Oxfordshire, Portsmouth. And on the other side you're lending £4m to Bedford at 6.42% and £5m to Surrey Heath at 5.50%, against money market funds at 3.71% to 3.84%. Being on both sides of the inter-authority market at a spread of over two points is unusual enough that it's worth having the sector-wide picture next to it. Our monthly PWLB breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is one half — July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — and we track short-term inter-authority pricing alongside it, so you can see where 6.42% sits against everyone else's before the next one comes round.

On training, four fit Cherwell. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator is the engine above with the workings shown, which given the £14.6m is probably the one. Debt restructuring sits next to it. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and LA Credit Analysis are for the Bedford and Surrey Heath side of Table 8. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
